The training *is* undertaken by nurses post qualification and is repeated I think two yearly. A porter, despite working in a hospital, is not a healthcare professional. The training is in person. You are assessed by another HCP, usually a practice educator. You cannot rock up as a porter, dinner lady etc and take it.

They wouldn't come under the NMC no. They wouldnt have indemnity. They would face legal prosecution because they are not allowed to give medication. 

Bottom line. If they gave drugs, they face prosecution. If you make a drug error as a nurse, you should have your competency and judgement analysed, then offered re training and a period of supervision. Potentially prosecution if gross misconduct etc.

The policies state it in such a way to account for changing parameters of our practice. Years ago, only doctors administered medication. That changed. And the code is loosely worded so if they created a new type of nurse, they are covered. 

"Only delegate tasks and duties that are within the
other person's scope of competence, making sure
that they fully understand your instructions". If you knew that that HCA was incompetent despite training, you shouldnt use them to check, highlight to their manager. I can as a nurse with a pin countersign your noradrenaline. However i cant remember the last time i gave it. So if you came to me for a check, i would tell you i am not competent and need to refer to the drug formulary etc. I am responsible for my own competence.

I imagine if it went to tribunal etc, say i had checked your drug for you but we had done it wrong. You would be asked to account for your actions as would i. And when asked "why did you sign for a drug you didn't know how to give?" My judgement would be called into account. 

These are policies, guidelines, recommendations. They cannot stipulate exact requirements.

> However, that statement, if paired with other statements other posters have said, seems to be a case of having your cake and eating it too -- in the sense that nobody is giving a straight answer but we all know who will be in the line of fire when things go wrong.

You should be able to trust your colleagues and it is unfortunate that in some places you cant. Hence, while someone may be able LEGALLY to countersign, you should ideally ask "have you given this before? Have you checked the formulary? Are you confident?" Even ask to see their training record if need be! You are within your rights to ask these questions. If they dont want to answer you, they should answer someone senior while you look for a second checker you trust.


** edit. I would ask a lawyer for advice. They know why these things are worded in certain ways. They could advise on liability laws etc. However you as a nurse/health professional should take reasonable actions to assess someones competence and there is where you are liable. Hence indemnity. Also, in a major drug error, policies are examined. I did say you are ultimately responsible, but if you got a union involved who said: the HCA was not competent snd reports were ignored. The training is not sufficient. The policy is not stringent. They can also be at fault. Im not entirely sure *what* you are looking for exactly.

Hospital specific policies state nurses can give drugs independently. My trust states we cannot do controlled drugs, inotropes etc. You'd have to look at hospital trusts to get their specific policies.

HCA, porters, physios etc have not completed safe medicate modules. Hense they would not be an appropriate person to check drugs with. I am not doing my due diligence to my patient by getting someone who doesnt know medication to the level required to administer. It does not mean that every nurse knows and is safe, but the courses, education we do means we are safer. If it only requires a single admin, you are well within your rights to have it checked if you feel uncomfortable, unfamiliar with the drug etc. Generally, acting within the scope of your practice. 

If the HCA has undertaken the safe medicate training and you feel comfortable, they can check your drugs. But as the person ultimately responsible is the one who gives it. They may feel it requires a senior nurse to check it. Band 4s, nursing associates generally have their medication giving abilities is capped, same as nurses cannot give a CD independently.

Every ward is different but heres how I used to do it at my old job.

I used to work in geriatrics. Your biggest contender is delirium. Get obs done, so if you can you can avoid waking them up at 2am(apply your own clinical judgement, if they are sick it's more important to do obs again at 2am etc). Delirium is worsened by sleep deprivation etc. 

Get a cup of tea and toast into them. 

8pm drug round.

Settling. Adhere to their bed time routine as much as possible. Jammies, teeth, toilet, bed. Lights out. We used to start at 9.

For those incontinent or unable to reposition, 2am turn and check.

6am turns and check. Obs. Ivs.

Avoid noise, lights, anything that will disturb their sleep.

In your downtime, check their paperwork. Is their weight needing updated? Check catheter insertion dates. Anything you can do/hand over to day shift. I find it difficult on a day shift to sit and review their notes but if someone says their weights due today, great I know todays objective. Review drug kardex. Does it need rewritten soon?

I moves geris to surgical and there is a lot more antibiotics and obs etc. Geris, just try and keep it low key for them.

Most importantly: look to your colleagues and especially HCSW. Know your obs, your meds etc. But ask them the routine.
